fields.expected: A sixth example, and the one closest to an AI and automation role, is a job-application agent I built in TypeScript and Node using Playwright. The problem was that applying to jobs is mostly repetitive browser work: opening ATS pages, refilling the same information, tracking state, following up. But a fully autonomous browser agent is dangerous here, since one wrong action can submit a real application or fabricate an answer in a legal or demographic field. So I built it as a deterministic, operator-controlled agent instead. Every application moves through an explicit state machine from DISCOVERED through QUEUED, FILL, READY_TO_SUBMIT, SUBMITTED, and I used SQLite as the single source of truth because automation gets unsafe when state diverges across processes. Mutating capabilities sit behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED that never default on. Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from auto-fill and always generate a human-review item. I also built an operator console for running and approving the pipeline, and I intentionally skip Workday and iCIMS rather than handle them unreliably. That tradeoff, deciding where automation should stop, is the part I would want to work on here.
